paras: The attempted lynching of William Hickson took place on the evening of 12 May 1903 on Whisky Chute in East St. Louis, Illinois, when a crowd of residents with a rope chased Hickson, a Black man, through several blocks. Alderman Frank Holten and a police roundsman stopped the mob and took Hickson to the police station, where he was locked up. It is known from a single report in the St. Louis Republic.

According to the Republic, Hickson had been drinking heavily early in the evening and came to believe that someone was trying to injure him. He obtained a revolver and flourished it in several places on Whisky Chute, chasing men and women out of stores and saloons. The paper added that the street's residents did not usually call the police to keep the peace but would "take the law in their own hands."

Residents organized what the paper called a "posse," secured a rope and chased Hickson for several blocks; the Republic described the pursuers as "an angry mob of blacks and whites." The paper reported that "it was said that several shots were fired," without saying who fired or at whom. Holten, driving by, asked about the excitement, caught Hickson and put him in his rig. With Roundsman Paddy Ryan, who had arrived in the meantime, he stood off the mob and delivered Hickson to the police station.
Hickson was locked up, but the coverage does not show whether he was charged, and no arrest of any member of the crowd was reported.

The St. Louis Republic ran the story on 13 May 1903 in its column of Illinois news under the headline "Alderman Prevents Negro's Lynching," with decks reading "Chase on Whisky Chute" and "Posse With Ropes Chases William Hickson." The account credited Holten with the rescue and gave Hickson's armed disturbance as the cause, while characterizing the neighborhood as one where residents took the law into their own hands. No other report of the episode, in either the white or the Black press, was found beyond this Republic item.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Hickson
bases: A1 reports a posse with a rope chasing Hickson and an alderman saving him 'from lynching', an attempted lynching with no death.

A1 describes an illegal crowd of residents who 'take the law in their own hands' pursuing Hickson with a rope after he flourished a revolver, but he was rescued and locked up alive, so no one was killed.
Only A1, a St. Louis Republic item, reports the episode; no second white or Black report was found (A2 is too general to tie to it).

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic report
accounts.gist: Hickson, drunk and fearing injury, flourished a revolver on Whisky Chute; residents formed a posse with a rope and chased him until Alderman Holten and Roundsman Ryan rescued him and jailed him.

framing.detail: The Republic's headline 'Alderman Prevents Negro's Lynching' centers the rescue; the story presents Hickson's armed disturbance as the cause and calls the crowd an 'angry mob' that takes 'the law in their own hands'.

sources.paper: The St. Louis Republic (St. Louis, Mo.)
sources.note: Only report found: 'Alderman Prevents Negro's Lynching'; posse with rope chases Hickson on Whisky Chute; Alderman Holten and Roundsman Ryan take him to the police station.
quotes: Alderman Frank Holten of East St. Louis last night saved William Hickson, an intoxicated negro, from lynching at the hands of an angry mob of blacks and whites on Whisky Chute
The residents of Whisky Chute do not usually call in the services of policemen to keep the peace, but take the law in their own hands.
A posse was organized, a rope was secured and the crowd started after the negro, chasing him several blocks.
It was said that several shots were fired, when Alderman Holten happened along.
